notes: Stake early and guard young shoots from slugs; cut back after flowering for a September repeat.

origin: Garden hybrids (L. polyphyllus: W North America)
notes: Short-lived; deadhead for a second flush. Prefers neutral to acid soil; watch for lupin aphid.

White bells with heavy maroon throats; seedlings revert to pink, so replant or resow. Toxic.
Short-lived, best grown as a biennial; strip rust-spotted lower leaves; stake in windy sites.
Karl Foerster's 'Flammenblume'; keep roots moist and thin weak stems to deter powdery mildew.
Pure white, strongly scented and highly mildew-resistant; lights up the late-summer border.
May need staking; Chelsea chop in late May for shorter, later plants; self-seeds lightly.
Evergreen basal rosettes; deadhead for repeat flowers; seeds gently into gaps in the border.
Dense violet heads; spreads by runners. Cut back after flowering for fresh leaves and a repeat.
Papery pincushion flowers for months; deadhead to limit seedlings; dislikes drying out.
Classic path edging; cut back hard after flowering for fresh leaves and to stop rampant self-seeding.
Sterile, so no seedlings; shear after flowering for fresh leaves; good red autumn tints.
Shear after the first flush for repeat flowers; sprawls, so give it a front-of-border spot.
Aromatic semi-evergreen mats for dry shade under trees; older leaves colour red in autumn.
Long-flowering magenta cranesbill for dry, sunny edges and rock gardens; red autumn leaves.
Dusky 'mourning widow' flowers for shade; cut back after flowering for fresh leaves; self-seeds.
Mildew-resistant late nectar for butterflies; Chelsea chop in late May to avoid staking.
Classic autumn aster; prone to mildew, so pick resistant cultivars and divide every 3 years.
Swiss-bred; lavender daisies from July to October. Leave stems over winter; divide only in spring.

origin: S & E Europe to C Asia
notes: Steel-blue globes beloved by bees; dries well. Deep taproot, so plant young and don't move it.

origin: C & SE Europe to C Asia
notes: Small metallic-blue thimbles on branched stems; needs lean, well-drained soil; dries well.
Plant rhizomes half-exposed to bake in the sun; divide every 3–4 years in July or August.
Classic pale-blue bearded iris, sweetly scented and vigorous; divide congested clumps after flowering.
Tough grassy clumps for moist soil; seed pods stand in winter; divide when the centre dies out.
Indestructible old farm-garden daylily; spreads by runners and is hard to remove once settled.
Rust-orange and yellow bicolour; tough and free-flowering. Each bloom lasts a day—snap off spent ones.
Orange-red pokers fading to yellow; needs good winter drainage. Don't cut leaves back in autumn.
Pleated sword leaves and flame-red flowers; divide congested clumps in spring to keep flowering.
French-raised pure white for late summer; slow to settle, then spreads by roots and is hard to remove.
Old German semi-double in silvery pink; spreads steadily in part shade and needs no staking.
Granny's bonnet; short-lived but self-seeds and hybridises freely. Cut back after flowering.
Spurless double pompons in rose, white and green; comes fairly true from seed if kept apart.
Farm-garden 'Tränendes Herz'; dormant by midsummer, so plant hostas or ferns to fill the gap.
Ferny blue-green leaves and cherry-red lockets for months; stays in leaf longer than bleeding heart.
Dies down after flowering—cut back and plant late fillers nearby. Resents disturbance.
Divide every 2–3 years to keep vigorous; deadhead for a long season of cutting daisies.
Burnt-orange heads fading to buff-yellow over grey-green ferny leaves; cut back after flowering.
Cerise-magenta yarrow; spreads by rhizomes, good in dry meadow-style plantings; colour fades with age.
Coppery-red daisies; Chelsea chop for sturdier stems; keep moist in summer, divide every 3 years.
German 'Summer Sun'; long-flowering golden daisies that rarely need staking; good for cutting.
Double lemon pompons; compact successor to the tall farm-garden 'Goldball'; needs no staking.
Carmine-red German cultivar with horizontal petals; leave cones for birds and winter structure.
Creamy white with a coppery-orange cone; short-lived in heavy soil that stays wet in winter.
Aromatic leaves and scarlet whorls; keep moist to limit mildew; divide every 3 years.
Dense blue spikes for the sunny front of the border; deadhead for repeat flowers.
'Blue Giantess': tall spires for moist borders; deadhead and it repeats; rarely needs staking.
Tiered whorls of leaves under lilac candelabra spires; no staking; seedheads stand all winter.
Crimson spikes from July to frost; weed-smothering clumps for moist soil; cut back in spring.
Dark-red buttons on wiry see-through stems for prairie planting; needs moisture-retentive soil.
Fluffy lilac clouds above columbine-like leaves; for moist part shade; self-seeds mildly.
Candyfloss-pink plumes for bog gardens and pond margins; spreads in wet soil; no staking.
Purple-backed leaves wilt in hot sun—site in moist part shade; protect young growth from slugs.
Georg Arends' dark-red classic; never let it dry out; leave the rusty seedheads for winter.
Tall, late magenta-purple plumes; copes with drier soil and more sun than × arendsii types.
Thick blue leaves resist slugs better than most; bluest in shade; lilac flowers in summer.
Crisp white-margined leaves brighten shade; slug-prone, so protect the young shoots in spring.
Huge chartreuse leaves thick enough to shrug off most slugs; tolerates more sun than most hostas.
Bronze-purple evergreen leaves; replant deeper when crowns turn woody; watch for vine weevil.
Ruffled lime-green evergreen leaves light up shade and pots; scorches in hot afternoon sun.
Silver-frosted heart-shaped leaves and forget-me-not flowers; scorches in sun or drought.

Spreads by runners into weed-proof mats; frothy white spring spikes; leaves bronze in winter.
Arching stems hung with green-tipped bells; check for sawfly larvae stripping the leaves in June.

Glossy purple-bronze rosettes spread by runners; blue spring spikes for bees; best colour in sun.
Glossy evergreen carpet under trees and shrubs; shear in early spring every few years to thicken.

Strawberry-like evergreen carpet with yellow spring stars; tough under trees in sun or shade.
Farm-garden staple with yellow spires; spreads fast in moist soil, so site it with care.
Karl Foerster's 'May Night' (1956); cut back after the first flush for a second flowering.
Plant buds no deeper than 5 cm or it won't flower; ring-stake the heavy double blooms.
Carmine-pink guard petals around a cream boss of petaloids; sturdy and needs little staking.
The old farm-garden peony, a fortnight before lactiflora; leave undisturbed for decades.
Plant the graft union 10–15 cm deep; slow and resents moving; shelter early buds from late frost.
Salmon-pink with a darker eye; clove-scented and repeat-flowering. Likes lime and sharp drainage.
Victorian white pink with intense clove scent; split calyx is normal; a classic path edging.

origin: C & E Europe to C Asia (cultivar)
notes: Clouds of tiny double white flowers; deep taproot—plant once in limy, free-draining soil.
'Brennende Liebe' of farm gardens; vivid scarlet heads; may need light support; deadhead.
Wine-red pincushions for months on floppy stems that weave through neighbours; self-seeds.

Spidery blue cornflowers; cut to the ground after the first flush for fresh leaves and a repeat.
Grey-green evergreen that flowers for months; short-lived, so root cuttings every 2–3 years.
Biennial; silvery moon-like seed discs for winter and dried arrangements; self-seeds freely.
Biennial carpet beneath tulips; pull out mildewed plants after flowering—it self-seeds.
Quilled pompon daisies grown as a biennial for spring pots and edging; deadhead to prolong.
Shear in midsummer for a fresh autumn flush; scrambles between roses and taller perennials.
Pale yellow spring flowers for hedge banks and woodland edges; divide clumps after flowering.
Mealy evergreen rosettes; scented flowers in many colours, shown in Victorian auricula theatres.

Lemon globes for damp soil by ponds or in bog gardens; cut back after flowering for fresh leaves.
Bold horse-chestnut leaves for bog or pond edges; shelter from wind and late spring frost.
Airy see-through stems turn butter-yellow in autumn, then break off at the base—little cutting back.
Compact clouds of gold-tinted flowers; one of few grasses for part shade; comb out in spring.
Cascading gold-striped leaves for shade and pots; slow to bulk up; turns russet in autumn.
White-edged evergreen sedge spreading slowly by runners; comb out tatty leaves in spring.
Olive leaves turn coppery-orange in sun and winter cold; short-lived, so replace every few years.
Red-tipped leaves turn deep burgundy in autumn; stands through winter; cut back in early spring.
Lime-green semi-evergreen matrix grass for sun or light shade; silvery spikes in late summer.
Evergreen hairy-leaved woodrush with snowy summer heads; copes with dry shade under trees.
Ernst Pagels selection; early red plumes ageing silver stand all winter; cut back in March.
Leaves banded crosswise in yellow once the weather warms; can flop in rich soil—don't feed.
Leaves redden from the tips to blood-red by autumn; dig out any green shoots that revert.
Lacy pale-green fronds for moist shade; shrivels in wind or drought; dies back in autumn.
Soft, finely cut evergreen fronds; tolerates dry shade once settled; cut old fronds in March.
Glossy strap-shaped evergreen fronds; happy on lime and in wall crevices; trim old fronds in spring.
Majestic fern for pond and stream edges; needs constantly wet, acid soil; russet in autumn.
Vase-shaped shuttlecocks; runs into colonies in moist soil; brown fertile fronds stand in winter.
Leathery evergreen fern for walls, banks and dry shade; new fronds appear in late summer.
Velvety maroon-black single late tulip; plant 15 cm deep in November; superb with white tulips.
Scented orange lily-flowered tulip; one of the most reliably perennial, often returning for years.
Double peony-flowered blush pink; heavy heads spoil in rain, so site in shelter or grow in pots.
Darwin hybrids are the most perennial large tulips; plant 20 cm deep and let leaves die back.
Low starry yellow-and-white tulip for rock gardens and gravel; naturalises in sunny spots.
Dwarf, early and multi-headed; ideal for pots, edges and rockeries; let leaves die back naturally.
Elegant multi-headed pure white triandrus; lightly scented; lovely among tulips and in grass.
Early cyclamineus daffodil with swept-back petals; reliable and naturalises well in grass.
Old pheasant's eye: the last daffodil to flower and intensely scented; naturalises in damp grass.
Plant 'in the green' just after flowering; spreads into drifts under deciduous trees and shrubs.

Large crocus striped lilac and white; naturalises in lawns—mow only once the leaves yellow.
Spreads into blue rivers along paths and under shrubs; its untidy leaves appear in autumn.
Intense blue bells carpet the ground under trees; self-seeds freely into lawns and beds.
Usually sold as Chionodoxa; upward-facing blue stars with white eyes; naturalises in sun.
Buy only nursery-raised bulbs; keep away from Spanish bluebell, which hybridises with it.
Chequered bells for damp meadow grass; naturalises where the soil stays moist in spring.
Farm-garden 'Kaiserkrone'; plant bulbs tilted 20 cm deep in rich, well-drained soil; foxy smell.
Tall snowflake from William Robinson's Gravetye; green-tipped bells; thrives in damp heavy soil.
Golden ruffs in late winter; buy in the green or soak tubers; spreads under deciduous trees.
Huge violet globes; strappy leaves wither at flowering, so hide them behind perennials.
Tall lilac drumsticks rising above peonies and catmint; seedheads stand well into summer.
Spires of starry blue flowers; naturalises in damp meadow grass and tolerates heavy clay.
Intensely fragrant white trumpets, purple outside; check for red lily beetle from spring.
Nodding Turk's caps; slow to establish but long-lived in light woodland. Resents being moved.
Plant just below the surface in late summer; keeps a leaf rosette over winter; prone to botrytis.
Near-black leaves and single scarlet flowers loved by bees; lift tubers after the first frost.
Dinnerplate blooms in blush and cream; stake firmly, disbud for size, lift tubers in autumn.
Plant corms in batches April–June for weeks of cut stems; stake; lift after frost and store dry.
Tender: start rhizomes indoors in spring and lift when frost blackens the leaves; bold foliage.
Heavily scented porcelain-blue spikes; looser in later years; good in pots and formal beds.
Soak the knobbly tubers overnight before planting; spreads into blue carpets under shrubs.
Magenta flowers in midwinter over silver-marked leaves; plant tubers shallowly under trees.
France's May Day muguet; spreads by rhizomes into dense colonies in shade. All parts toxic.
